subject: Civil Engineering
title: What Is a Truss?
description: A quick, practical guide to What Is a Truss?.

hook.text: Look at a crane arm — it's not solid. It's a skeleton of triangles.

buildup.text: A truss is a framework of bars connected at joints. Each bar carries only axial force.

discovery.text: Triangles are rigid — they can't deform without breaking a member. Rectangles can.

twist.text: That's why bridges, roofs, and towers are all built from triangulated shapes.

climax.text: The Eiffel Tower is one massive truss — 18,000 iron parts forming rigid triangles.

punchline.text: Triangles can't be pushed out of shape. That's the secret.

quiz.question: Why are triangles used as the basic shape in trusses?
options: They use less material than other shapes
They are inherently rigid and cannot deform without breaking a member
They distribute weight evenly to all corners

details.summary: A truss is a structural framework of triangular units made from straight members connected at joints. Each member carries only axial tension or compression, making trusses extremely efficient for spanning long distances.
details.whyItMatters: Trusses span far greater distances than solid beams using a fraction of the material. They are fundamental to roof systems, bridges, transmission towers, and crane structures worldwide.
takeaways: Triangles are the only polygon that cannot deform without changing member lengths
Truss members carry only axial forces, either pure tension or pure compression
Truss depth provides the lever arm that resists bending across the entire span

faq.question: Why are triangles used in trusses instead of rectangles or other shapes?
faq.answer: A triangle has three sides and three joints, and it cannot change shape without changing the length of at least one member. A rectangle with pin joints can collapse into a parallelogram because its opposite sides can rotate freely.

faq.question: How does a truss resist bending even though each member carries only axial force?
faq.answer: The top and bottom chords of a truss act like the top and bottom of a beam, with the top chord in compression and the bottom in tension for a loaded truss. The web members connect them and transfer shear forces.
